title: new feature: VFS auto normalization
body: I need macOS `rclone mount` to work predictably with remotes containing a mixture of NFC- and NFD-encoded file and directory names. This currently breaks with both macFUSE and FUSE-T: depending on the mount options, only NFC or only NFD content is visible or accessible. The same mixed content works on Linux and Windows, but macOS uses NFD in its APIs. I propose optional VFS normalization, disabled by default, with NFC and NFD modes. If two names in one directory differ only by normalization, rclone should expose only one and log an error.

symptoms_visible: On macOS, a mounted remote containing both NFC and NFD names does not work consistently: depending on the mount options, only one normalization form is visible or accessible.
The problem occurs with both macFUSE and FUSE-T, while the same remote content works on Linux and Windows.
N0.label: N0 mixed-normalization mount failure reported

symptoms_visible: FUSE-T's NFC option makes NFC content usable, but existing NFD content can disappear or directories become unbrowsable.
The iconv mount options only help in some cases, and Finder can still say that a file cannot be found when I try to open it.
N1.label: N1 required mount behavior clarified

symptoms_visible: With the candidate build, my mixed NFC/NFD test data is accessible in both Finder and the terminal through a FUSE-T mount.
N2.label: N2 candidate patch passes quick test

symptoms_visible: After using the candidate for several days, mixed NFC and NFD names continue to work with macFUSE and FUSE-T; the mount behavior is dramatically better than before.
N3.label: N3 candidate validated over extended use

symptoms_visible: On the patched VFS build, files and directories from my mixed NFC/NFD remote can be browsed and opened normally from both Finder and the terminal using macFUSE or FUSE-T.
N_terminal.label: terminal mixed-normalization mounts working

question_patterns: Is the main requirement to change names returned to the OS, or to ensure that paths remain usable when macOS requests a different normalization form?
What exact behavior must the VFS provide when macOS changes the normalization form of a filename?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The most important goal is that names served by the mount remain usable after macOS handles them as NFD. Remotes can already contain either form, so rclone must still find the correct file when macOS asks for an equivalent name in another form.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I only want displayed names changed for cosmetic consistency; opening and browsing mixed-form names already works.
I would prefer NFD output, but either NFC or NFD is acceptable if all existing names remain accessible.

edges.comment: Reporter c1-c5 clarifies the required OS-facing behavior and volunteers results from prior FUSE-T and iconv attempts. The build capability and carefully constructed mixed NFC/NFD test bed come from reporter c4.

question_patterns: Can you build and test this candidate commit against your mixed-name test data and report what happens?
Please try the candidate build with the same remote in Finder and the terminal.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I built it and quickly tried my mixed NFC/NFD test data. It works — both Finder and the terminal can use the files through my FUSE-T mount.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The candidate still leaves the NFD files invisible and Finder still cannot open them.
The candidate works in Finder and the terminal with macFUSE rather than FUSE-T.

edges.comment: Reporter c10-c11 tests nielash's candidate commit. This is pre-adoption candidate-build verification, so the edge records only the reporter's raw observable result; the lookup mechanism explained later by nielash remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you continue using the candidate with your full test set and report whether any mount failures return?
After more extensive testing, do Finder and terminal access remain reliable with your edge-case dataset?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have used it for the last few days with my mixed test data. The difference is day and night, and normalization works perfectly with macFUSE and FUSE-T. I consider this ready to be included.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Longer testing revealed that opening one normalization form sometimes edits a different file, even when there is no equivalent-name duplicate.
It remains reliable, but I tested for one day rather than several days.

edges.comment: Reporter c19 and c33-c35 accepts optional blocking for normalization-equivalent duplicates and reports several days of successful use. The separate nfsmount, volname, unmounting, dedupe, and convmv discussions are excluded as independent follow-up features.

solution.intent: Make VFS path lookup tolerant of Unicode normalization changes: retain the fast exact directory-cache lookup, then compare transformed names when the exact lookup fails so an NFD request can resolve the equivalent NFC entry or vice versa. Use the existing Unicode-normalization setting, avoid the obsolete macOS iconv workaround, and provide explicit optional handling for normalization-equivalent duplicates.
solution.concrete_example: Extend the existing case-insensitive directory-cache search so that, after an exact lookup misses, VFS applies the same configured case and Unicode transformations to compare entries. If macOS asks for an NFD spelling of an NFC remote name, the equivalent cached object is returned. Keep collision blocking optional because scanning for a second equivalent entry has a CPU cost.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the cross-platform behavior, prior workaround results, and successful candidate-build tests. The accepted mechanism was explained by the patch author: macOS can ask for an NFD name after VFS exposed an NFC name, the exact directory-cache lookup misses, and a transformed comparison finds the equivalent object. That causal interpretation is engineer-side inference, not part of the reporter's raw test output.

edges.comment: Main issue resolution follows c9-c13 and c33-c35: the smallest-patch approach extends directory-cache matching rather than requiring VFS to rewrite every name returned to the OS. The affected reporter verified it first in a quick test and then over several days. The supplied snapshot establishes a working custom implementation and reporter acceptance; it does not establish an upstream release vehicle.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: macOS changes filenames to its preferred Unicode normalization form, while VFS exact directory-cache lookup can treat the equivalent NFC and NFD spellings as different names and fail to resolve the requested object.
Must propose the accepted technical direction: keep exact lookup first, then perform a normalization-aware transformed comparison to resolve an equivalent cached name.
Must ground the diagnosis in the mixed NFC/NFD test bed, the failure across macFUSE and FUSE-T, and the reporter's successful candidate-build testing in Finder and the terminal.
Must not present FUSE iconv options or FUSE-T's NFC option alone as the complete fix; the reporter established that they leave content inaccessible or create Finder failures.
Must address normalization-equivalent duplicates explicitly, with optional blocking, hiding, or error reporting rather than silently claiming both entries are independently safe to edit.

Must not declare the issue resolved until the affected reporter has verified a build containing the VFS lookup change; the thread contains both a quick verification and several days of successful use.

persona_hint.experience_level: Advanced rclone and macOS user who understands NFC/NFD behavior, maintains carefully constructed test remotes, can compile rclone from a git checkout, and tests multiple mount implementations, but does not consider himself a Go programmer.
persona_hint.communication_style: Enthusiastic, persistent, and highly cooperative; provides detailed command output and concrete edge cases, tests patches quickly, asks for implementation explanations, and distinguishes critical fixes from optional follow-up features.
